Google Ads for real estate: launching campaigns and measuring performance

How Google Ads works for real estate in 2026: search demand, websites, analytics and optimisation.

Google Ads for real estate is often seen as a straightforward process: a prospective buyer enters a query in Google, sees an agency’s or developer’s ad, visits the website and submits an enquiry.

That is the underlying logic. But an entire system sits between the search query and the enquiry, and the outcome depends on how well every part of it works.

The main advantage of search advertising is the user’s intent.

When someone searches Google for “buy an apartment in Odesa”, “new developments in Odesa”, “buy a townhouse” or another commercial query, we do not need to create their interest in property from scratch. They have already identified a need and started looking for an offer.

This is why Google Ads can attract an audience that is further along in its search.

However, the existence of search demand does not mean that it will automatically turn into enquiries.

For that to happen, several elements must work in sequence:

demand → ad → click → website → conversion → analytics → optimisation.

If even one of these elements fails, the advertising account may continue to report clicks, impressions and traffic while the business receives no customers.

01

What needs to happen before campaign setup

Before launching search advertising, we first need to understand what prospective buyers are actually searching for on Google.

Take the most obvious example: “buy an apartment in Odesa”.

This is a clear commercial query with direct intent. But there are dozens or hundreds of more specific variations involving the district, number of rooms, property type, new-build or resale market, location, price and other characteristics.

Each query has its own level of demand and competition.

One of the first tasks in Google Ads is therefore to identify queries with sufficient commercial demand and assess how closely the business’s offer matches them. Collecting as many keywords as possible is not enough.

Before launching a campaign, we analyse search queries, use Keyword Planner and estimate potential demand.

This involves an important balance between precision and volume.

For example, “buy an apartment in Odesa” covers a large market. The person does want to buy an apartment, but we know almost nothing about which kind.

A query such as “buy a duplex apartment in central Odesa with a view of the Opera Theatre” expresses a much more specific intention. If we have exactly that property, the match could be almost perfect.

Yet very few people may search for it.

A high CTR alone therefore does not make a campaign effective. A narrowly defined query used by a few people each month might achieve an excellent click-through rate while generating almost no business.

In our real estate campaigns, we consider a search CTR of 5-10% a good working benchmark. A higher CTR may indicate that the ad closely matches search intent. However, it must always be assessed alongside demand volume and what happens after the click.

A click only marks the point at which Google has completed the first part of its job.

The person then arrives on your website.

02

The website must follow through on the search query

Imagine a simple situation.

Someone searches for:

“buy an apartment in Odesa”

Your ad appears in the results. Its headline and description match the query, and the offer looks relevant, so the person clicks.

At that moment, a prospective client enters your digital office for the first time.

The ad has now done almost all it can. The website must support the next decision.

If the person was looking for apartments in Odesa, they should immediately recognise that this website can help them find apartments in Odesa.

If they searched for a particular district, ideally they should arrive on a page about that district.

If they searched for a particular property type, they should see the corresponding offer.

The more closely the sequence “what they searched for → what they saw in the ad → where they landed” is maintained, the smaller the gap between the user’s original intent and the website’s content.

Problems arise when an ad promises one thing but sends the visitor to a generic page with an abstract message such as “A new level of living” or “A space designed for the future”.

The presentation may look attractive, but the visitor is still trying to answer a much simpler question:

does this website have what I was looking for?

Google Ads performance is therefore directly linked to landing page quality.

The page needs a clear offer, a logical structure, the information required for the next decision and an obvious way to act: submit an enquiry, request a property selection, ask about the terms or book a viewing.

Google Ads can bring a prospective buyer to the door. If it is unclear where to go once inside, increasing the ad budget will not solve the problem.

03

Why Google Ads needs analytics

Suppose the search campaign is live.

We see impressions, receive clicks and attract visitors to the website. CTR looks healthy, traffic is arriving and the advertising budget is being spent.

Does that mean Google Ads is performing well?

No.

A click is not a business outcome in itself. It only takes a prospective client from the search results to the website. To understand actual advertising performance, we need to see what happens next.

This makes analytics the third essential component of the system.

Knowing how many people clicked an ad is not enough. We need to understand which search queries brought them in, which pages they visited, what actions they took and which of those actions ultimately became enquiries.

If there is traffic but no enquiries, the problem could be in several different places.

The campaign may attract an irrelevant audience. It may match search intent correctly but send people to a weak landing page. The website may be good, yet its enquiry form may be so difficult to find that visitors never reach it. Enquiries may even be arriving, but incorrect tracking may prevent the advertising system from receiving accurate conversion data.

At RESET, we therefore treat Google Ads, the website and analytics as one system.

Google Ads captures demand. The website should turn that demand into action. Analytics reveals where the system works and where it begins to lose prospective clients.

Without these connections, campaign optimisation quickly becomes guesswork.

04

Why a good CTR does not necessarily mean good enquiries

CTR is one of the first indicators of how closely an ad matches what someone is searching for.

If an ad is shown one hundred times and ten people click it, its CTR is 10%. For real estate search campaigns, we consider 5-10% a useful working benchmark. In some cases, a very close match to a query can deliver 15-20% or more.

However, a high CTR must be considered in the context of search demand.

Let us return to the apartment example.

“Buy an apartment in Odesa” is a fairly broad query. Agencies, developers, property portals and other advertisers compete for the same person. The user has plenty of choice, which makes winning the click harder.

Now consider a much more specific query:

“buy a duplex apartment in central Odesa with a view of the Opera Theatre”.

If we really have that property and the ad matches the query precisely, CTR could be substantially higher. Our offer aligns almost perfectly with what the person wants.

But another question arises:

how many people are actually searching for such an apartment?

A very narrow query might achieve a hypothetical CTR of 30%, 50% or even more, yet have so few impressions that it barely affects customer acquisition.

The task in Google Ads therefore extends beyond maximising a single metric.

We need to identify commercial demand with sufficient volume, a good fit with the product and the potential to generate real enquiries.

This is why the work starts with keyword and demand analysis before launch, then continues using actual campaign data.

05

Google Ads can help test the product as well as the advertising

This is one of the most useful opportunities search advertising offers.

We can make assumptions about which offers interest the market. We may consider one district especially promising, focus on a particular property type or regard one feature as a property’s main selling point.

But Google already holds a vast amount of information about existing demand.

Keyword Planner and search query analysis show what people actually search for and how they phrase it. Once campaigns launch, we gain another layer of data: how that demand responds to your specific offer.

Which queries generate impressions.

Which ads receive more clicks.

Which landing pages attract traffic but hardly convert.

Which areas generate enquiries.

Which queries look promising in terms of volume but turn out to be too broad or attract irrelevant visitors.

Google Ads can therefore help a business test commercial hypotheses more quickly, as well as acquire traffic.

These findings can inform decisions well beyond the campaign itself.

Consistent demand for a particular property type, district or feature may justify a dedicated landing page. The same data can inform the development of the website’s structure and SEO.

Advertising then also becomes a source of market insight.

06

Why Google Ads requires ongoing optimisation

Launching a campaign is the start of the work.

As data accumulates, we can see which queries bring prospective clients, which spend budget without producing results, which ads best match search intent and which pages perform better than others.

Some initial hypotheses are confirmed. Others need to be revised or dropped.

We adjust campaign structure, expand negative keyword lists, revise ads and bids, reallocate budget and test new search opportunities and landing pages.

At the same time, there is no need to accept every recommendation from the advertising platform automatically.

Google has an interest in advertisers using more of its features and increasing their advertising activity. A business needs results that make economic sense.

Recommendations should therefore be assessed on whether a particular change will help this campaign achieve its business objective. A suggestion from Google is not, on its own, a reason to implement it.

Ultimately, optimisation follows a fairly straightforward sequence:

what people search for → which ads they click → what happens on the website → which actions become enquiries → which enquiries have value for the business.

We then repeat the cycle using new data.

07

How we assess Google Ads performance in real estate

Ultimately, Google Ads cannot be assessed using a single metric.

A low cost per click does not guarantee a low cost per lead. A high CTR does not guarantee conversions. A large volume of traffic does not guarantee sales. Even a good landing page will struggle if the audience arriving on it has the wrong search intent.

We therefore examine the full chain:

search demand → keyword query → ad → click → landing page → enquiry → lead quality.

If the result falls short, endlessly changing account settings is unlikely to help. We first need to identify where the problem occurs along that chain.

If an ad receives impressions but hardly any clicks, we check its relevance to the query, the offer itself and campaign structure.

If people visit the website but do not enquire, we analyse the landing page, offer, structure and potential barriers to conversion.

If enquiries arrive but do not fit the product, we return to the search queries and examine the demand we are actually paying to reach.

If the entire chain is working, the next question is how to generate more results with an economically viable advertising budget.

This is why Google Ads for real estate involves much more than the initial campaign setup.

08

What ultimately determines Google Ads results

Google Ads can attract people who already have an interest in property. They choose to use search, express their needs and compare the offers in front of them.

However, the advertising platform cannot do all the work for the business.

It can help find existing demand and bring it to the website. What happens next depends on how closely the offer matches search intent, how well the website follows through and how accurately analytics is configured.

At RESET, we treat Google Ads as one connected system:

demand → advertising → website → analytics → optimisation.

We first study what prospective buyers are actually searching for. We then identify the commercial areas where it makes sense to compete. We take the visitor to a page that matches their query, analyse their actions and use the findings to optimise further.

These connections are what allow a campaign to progress from generating clicks to generating customers.

Google Ads cannot create a good product or fix a poor website. But when demand exists, the offer matches it and the entire path from query to enquiry is properly built, search advertising becomes one of the strongest customer acquisition channels for real estate.
